chapter.title: Professor Grant
chapter.sub: Three years of recordings that fade at the whiteboard — and a dashboard that stayed green the whole time.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT · CASE-028  Cold case · Professor Grant, Maya and Wes · Level L4 · Intermediate support  For three years Professor Grant has said his lecture recordings fade whenever he walks to the whiteboard. For three years he has been shown a green dashboard.  ⚑ RV-130: auto-mixer simplified. RV-131: levels, not listening. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Professor Grant
items.stakes: A professor has reported the same fault for three years and been shown the same green dashboard every time. He is out of patience, and he is right.
items.reward: Recordings that hold steady wherever Grant stands. A dashboard that checks what students get. Grant's trust — from almost nothing.

objectives.text: Bring the whiteboard into the recording
Look closer: two things about Hall D

items.rumor: The dashboard isn't lying. It's answering a different question.

items.alt: A recording's level over time: tall and full while Grant is at the lectern, collapsing to a thin line in two shaded stretches labeled 'at the board'.
items.caption: Organic chemistry. The reaction mechanisms are on the whiteboard. In the recording, that's where he disappears.

lines.text: I have filed eleven tickets. I have been told eleven times that the microphones are working.
They probably were. That's not the same as you being heard.

items.alt: The AV office. Professor Grant, gray-bearded, stands at Maya's desk; behind them the wall of room tiles is entirely green.

bubbles.text: Eleven tickets. Three years. Every one closed ‘no fault found’.
Then we've been looking at the wrong thing.

items.prompt: Are you going to show me the green screen too?

options.label: “No. I'm going to ask you to show me. Can we record you walking the room — now?”
options.reply: …Nobody has asked me to show them. Lead the way.

options.label: “The dashboard does say the mics are fine.”
options.reply: Then the dashboard and I have nothing further to discuss.

options.label: “What exactly happens when you go to the board?”
options.reply: My students tell me I become a ghost. Their word.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  How far is too far from the microphone?  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Grant beside a board. Inverse square: level drops twenty log of d-two over d-one. From one metre to four, that's twelve dB. So when I walk to the whiteboard the microphone thinks I've left the room. The auto-mixer does, yes. For three years.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Auto-mixer   Coverage   Pickup lobe   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Inverse-square law  ΔL = 20·log 10 (d 2  ÷ d 1 )   d 1   starting distance  d 2   new distance  ΔL  level lost, dB     ƒ FORMULA · Open microphones and gain before feedback  ΔGBF = −10·log 10 (N open )   N open   how many times more mics are open  ΔGBF  change in gain before feedback, dB

items.prompt: 1:55. Grant is at your desk with three years of tickets. What do you do?
items.risk: Grant stops reporting — and 240 students keep revising from ghost recordings.
timeout: He was offering you the evidence.

options.label: Show him the dashboard: the mics are online
options.result: Grant: “That is exactly what I was shown last year.” He leaves.
options.consequence: The proxy again, to the one person who knows the outcome.

options.label: Ask him to show you: record a walk test with him in Hall D, now
options.result: Grant, surprised: “Nobody has asked me to show them.” At the board: 12 dB down, then the mixer gates him out.
options.consequence: The person reporting the outcome is your best instrument.

options.label: Give him a lapel mic
options.result: He wears it Tuesday, forgets it Thursday.

options.label: Open ticket #12
options.result: It is closed in two days: ‘no fault found’.
options.consequence: The same process, the same result.

items.alt: Hall D. Grant at the whiteboard, pointing at a mechanism; Maya at the lectern with a tablet showing the recording level: minus 12 dB, gated.

bubbles.text: At the lectern: fine. Here: twelve dB down, and the mixer decides you've left.
I have not left. I am teaching the important part.

items.title: Green for three years.
items.body: The dashboard has been green every day Grant complained. Mic online, file exists — and since the spring (S05E01), ‘audio present’, averaged over the whole hour. Grant's loud lectern minutes carry the average. The check fixed after Engineering's silent recordings can't see a professor who fades for ten minutes at a time.
items.label: Test: what does green actually rule out?

items.alt: The dashboard's check list for Hall D: mic array online, recording file exists, audio present averaged over the hour — all ticked green. Speech steady throughout: not checked.
items.caption: The spring's audio check averages the hour. Grant's loud minutes hide his silent ones.

items.title: Closed · ‘no fault found’
items.body: Grant's eleventh ticket, closed eight months ago: *Checked dashboard. Mic online, recordings present. No fault found.* Every ticket closed the same way, by a different person, each checking the same two things. Maya reads all eleven. Wes: “We kept asking the dashboard instead of him.”

items.label: **Learn it now:** auto-mixers, coverage and open microphones.

items.alt: Hall D's commissioning file, three years old: lobe 3 at the whiteboard switched off because of ventilation noise, with a note to revisit after the ventilation was balanced.
items.caption: Facilities rebalanced the ventilation two years ago. Nobody revisited.

items.title: Lobe 3 was always there.
items.body: The array has a lobe aimed at the whiteboard. It was switched off at installation because the ventilation was noisy, with a note: *revisit after HVAC balance.* Facilities balanced it two years ago. The fix was one setting and one walk test away — for two years.
items.label: Test: what went wrong — and why not open everything?

items.prompt: 3:15. The ventilation noise is gone. How do you cover the whiteboard?
timeout: Thursday arrives with lobe 3 still off.

hints.text: What does each extra open microphone cost?

options.label: Turn every lobe on at full gain
options.result: The room hisses, the PA rings at 2.1 kHz, the lectern goes thin.
options.consequence: More open mics cost gain before feedback.
options.fail: Cover where people stand, not everywhere.

options.label: Enable lobe 3 aimed at the board, set its gain from the walk test, and check the auto-mixer keeps open mics low
options.result: Lobe 3 opens when he's at the board, closes when he's back at the lectern.
options.consequence: Coverage where he stands, headroom kept.

options.label: Ask Grant to teach from the lectern
options.result: He moves the mechanisms to slides. His students say they understand less.
options.consequence: Changes his teaching to fit our room.

options.label: Replace the array
options.result: Nine weeks and a budget request.

items.title: The first public-address systems
items.body: In the early 1920s, amplified public-address systems let a single speaker be heard by crowds of thousands — as long as he stayed at the microphone. Step back and the sound fell away, exactly as the inverse square predicts. A hundred years later, lecturers still walk out of their microphones' reach.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #47 · AVERY'S LENS  Measure the outcome, not the proxy  A status check should ask whether the person got what they came for — not only whether the device is on.  Hall D's dashboard checked that the mic was online and a file existed. For three years, neither was the problem.

items.alt: System View of Hall D from above: the lectern lobe covers the lectern; the whiteboard lobe is dashed and off; Grant's path to the board leaves every open lobe, 4 m out, −12 dB, gated.
items.caption: He isn't quiet. He's outside the room's hearing.

lines.text: Lobe three was just… off? The whole time?
With a note saying ‘revisit’. Nobody owned the word.

items.label: **Fix it:** bring the whiteboard into the recording.

items.prompt: Wednesday. What should the dashboard check from now on?
timeout: The dashboard stays as it is.
It stays green over the next Grant.

hints.text: What would have turned Grant's first ticket red?

options.label: Speech level minute by minute in every recording, flagging any fade longer than a minute — levels only, agreed with the teaching office — and a ‘revisit’ field with an owner and a date in every commissioning file
options.result: Night one: 37 rooms fade somewhere. Nobody listened to a single lecture.
options.consequence: Green now means students can hear.

options.label: Raise the hour-average threshold
options.result: Grant still passes: his lectern minutes carry any average.
options.consequence: A stricter average is still an average.

options.label: Wait for complaints
options.consequence: The people who give up stop complaining.

options.label: Listen to a sample of lectures every week
options.result: The faculty union hears about it by Friday.

items.alt: System View after the fix: lobe 3 on at the whiteboard; Grant's path stays inside an open lobe the whole way. Steady.
items.caption: Thursday's walk test: within 3 dB from lectern to board.

items.alt: Hall D after Thursday's lecture. Grant listens to the recording on headphones, smiling; Maya beside him.

bubbles.text: There. The end of my sentence. First time in three years.
Thank you for not giving up on telling us.

items.title: Forwarded by Grant
items.body: Grant forwards an email from a student, sent after Thursday: *Professor — the recording worked today. I'm deaf in one ear and I revise from these. I never heard your mechanisms before, only the lectern parts.* Grant's note on top: *Please pass this to whoever fixed it.*

items.alt: The campus quad at midday, the signage kiosk in the middle of the path. Delgado on his phone beside it.

bubbles.text: Noon test of the emergency alerts. The shelter message took a minute and a half to reach these signs. The phones had it in five seconds.

items.caption: Next: *Signal, Delayed.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Distance costs about 6 dB per doubling: cover where people actually stand, and remember every extra open mic costs headroom. A dashboard should check the outcome — speech in the recording — not only that the device is on. Revisits need owners and dates.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Grant filed eleven tickets. What makes someone stop reporting a problem — and how would you know they had?
